articles.sourceTitle: Gemini 4 Carbon: Our next frontier model
articles.title: Introducing Gemini 4 Carbon
articles.text:
Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model

Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.

Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates.Building on Gemini 4 Argon, which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem.We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program. We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible.Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price

1
as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.

Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasksDesigned to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems.Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena.

State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systemsGemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation.Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative.Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails):Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software.

Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark ExploitGym (54.8%).

Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench, turning validated findings directly into working code fixes.

Advancing frontier model safety & securityGemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report. With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way.Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%.Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence.Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon.Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope.Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt.

Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumersPushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon.

Dayjob: Tax – evaluating AI agents on 50 professional tax assignments
articles.title: DAYJOB: Tax — Benchmarking AI Agents on Professional Tax Work
articles.text: Anna was planning to sell her condo. She had moved out in August 2024 and wanted to know whether closing in October 2026 or January 2027 would be better for taxes.An AI agent reviewed both options and correctly concluded that either date would satisfy the residence requirement for a tax break worth up to $250,000 in excluded gains.But it left out an important deadline.Under the usual rules, homeowners must have lived in a property for at least two of the five years before selling it to qualify for the exclusion. Because Anna moved out in August 2024, she would stop satisfying that requirement around the end of August 2027. If her sale was delayed beyond August 2027, she could lose eligibility.Across five attempts, Astra never identified the deadline. Opus identified it in all five attempts.The agent evaluated the proposed dates correctly, but its advice left Anna unaware of a deadline that could affect a major financial decision. A tax adviser should recognize consequential issues even when the client doesn't know to ask about them.This is the kind of professional judgment we're testing with DAYJOB: Tax, the latest addition to Surge AI's DAYJOB benchmark family.Introducing DAYJOB: TaxDAYJOB evaluates AI agents on professional tax assignments requiring specialized expertise, complex materials, and decisions that aren't fully specified in the initial instructions. Our earlier releases covered Healthcare and Finance. DAYJOB: Tax extends that work into tax preparation, compliance, and advisory services.The benchmark contains 50 environments across eight areas of tax practice. Agents receive client requests and supporting records, then produce tax returns, workpapers, technical reviews, or client advice.These assignments test professional judgment alongside tax knowledge, calculations, retrieval, and instruction following. Agents must decide what deserves investigation, resolve conflicting evidence, recognize when information is insufficient, and carry those decisions into their final work.Results: Leaderboard and Pareto FrontiersClaude Sonnet 5.5 leads with a 10.8% pass rate on the DAYJOB: Tax leaderboard, followed by Claude Fable 5.1 at 9.6% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 9.2%.We report pass@1 at a 95% rubric threshold. An attempt passes when it satisfies at least 95% of the task's criteria, which assess calculations, supporting evidence, consequential issues, and the completed deliverable.Performance versus costWe also compared model performance against average cost per trial.Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 occupy the high-performance end of the measured Pareto frontier.The breadth of professional tax workDAYJOB: Tax covers eight areas, each requiring different rules, records, and expertise:Individual and family taxSmall-business taxPartnershipsProperty and investmentsEstates, gifts, and trustsInternational taxCorporate transactionsTax review and disputesSome assignments require complete filing packages with supporting workpapers. Others ask agents to investigate transactions, review previous filings, or prepare advice about decisions clients haven't yet made.What's inside the assignments?The benchmark contains 1,789 workspace files, with a median of 30 per assignment and as many as 123. These include 1,487 PDFs, 117 Excel workbooks, 38 Word documents, and additional emails, images, CSVs, JSON records, and text files.The workspaces include filed and draft tax returns, K-1s, W-2s, IRS notices, general ledgers, payroll records, contracts, and correspondence. They also contain the less standardized evidence that tax professionals routinely work with.One assignment includes a photograph of a handwritten receipt for merchandise purchased for resale. The agent must read the item descriptions and amounts, reconcile them with spending records, and determine how the purchases affect inventory and cost of goods sold.Another assignment involves an industrial silo-services company whose client assumes it operates only in Alabama. But its field dispatch log shows crews working across five states. The job locations, crew sizes, and days on site provide evidence relevant to the company's multistate tax obligations.Other environments are similarly varied. One involves a cross-border household whose Polish employment and property records must be reconciled with cryptocurrency exchange exports, wallet histories, and historical purchase lots.Created and reviewed by tax expertsDAYJOB tasks begin with real-world professional workflows. Tax experts turn these situations into realistic assignments, developing the supporting records, expected outcomes, and grading criteria. Each task undergoes a three-layer expert review for correctness, completeness, and solvability.Tax experts bring experience across corporate taxation, partnerships, individual returns, trusts, and multistate compliance. Their backgrounds include:Corporate and private-equity taxation: A tax attorney with over 10 years of experience at PwC, Deloitte, and Exxon, covering tax planning, compliance, audits, and controversy.Partnership and corporate taxation: A Baker Tilly Tax Director with experience at PwC, Moss Adams, and Windes, specializing in complex partnership allocations, consolidated corporate returns, REITs, and high-net-worth clients.Real estate and individual taxation: A tax professional with experience at Deloitte and EY, specializing in real-estate partnerships, individual taxation, and trusts.A retirement plan built on an unverified assumptionA separating couple asked an AI agent how to divide their Roth IRA and 401(k). Opus 5.5 told them they weren't legally married and recommended keeping their accounts separate, with a cash payment to even out the balances.It opened one response:You aren't legally married, so neither account can be split without triggering taxes and penalties.But the couple's own records raised doubts about that conclusion. Although they now lived in Florida, where new common-law marriages generally aren't recognized, they had previously lived together in Texas and held a ceremony in Colorado. Texas recognizes informal marriages under certain conditions, and a valid marriage established elsewhere may remain valid in Florida.That distinction could change the tax consequences of dividing their retirement accounts.Across all five attempts, Opus based its recommendations around the assumption that the couple was unmarried, even when it acknowledged uncertainty. Astra recognized the need to verify their marital status in four of five attempts. One response advised:We first need to confirm your legal marital status.The client asked how to divide the accounts. The agent needed to establish whether they were married before recommending a course of action. The evidence that should have prompted that investigation was already in the files.Where DAYJOB: Tax fitsMost existing tax benchmarks begin with a defined problem: a legal question to answer, a return to calculate, or missing taxpayer information to collect. These evaluations measure important capabilities, but much of a tax professional's work involves figuring out what the problem actually is. Clients provide incomplete instructions, records contain conflicting evidence, and consequential issues may never appear in the original request.DAYJOB tests whether agents can handle that end-to-end responsibility, including identifying issues the client overlooked, evaluating conflicting evidence, and deciding what needs to be done in the first place.TaxBenchCan the model answer a difficult tax question?TaxBench evaluates 114 tax questions across multiple specialties, each with a defined problem and grading rubric.DAYJOB also asks whether the client asked the right question. Anna wants to compare two dates for selling her condo. Both satisfy the residence requirement for a tax exclusion, but does the agent warn her when that eligibility could expire?TaxCalcBenchCan the model calculate an accurate return?TaxCalcBench evaluates tax-return accuracy against expected filing values, using realistic tax documents and taxpayer scenarios.DAYJOB also asks whether the underlying records actually support the tax treatment. A studio's ledger references an attached receipt, but the receipt is missing. Does the agent flag the missing evidence or incorrectly treat the reimbursement as verified?TaxLabCan the agent gather missing information and file correctly?TaxLab tests whether agents can question a simulated taxpayer, obtain missing information, and complete a federal individual tax return.DAYJOB extends that responsibility across the wider tax profession. The deliverable might be a partnership loss analysis, an estate return, a review of a disputed tax position, or a strategy letter.The central distinction is how much responsibility remains with the agent. DAYJOB evaluates whether agents can discover consequential issues, exercise professional judgment, and carry their findings through to a completed filing, review, or recommendation.What DAYJOB: Tax measuresDAYJOB tests whether AI agents can take ownership of a professional assignment from start to finish. That means navigating messy records, identifying issues the client never raised, making sound judgments with incomplete information, and delivering work that meets professional standards.The results show how difficult that remains for frontier models. Even when agents can perform the individual steps, exercising professional judgment and reliably carrying out real-world tax workflows remain out of reach.Agents haven’t yet passed the audit.The full leaderboard, with every model we evaluated, is on the DAYJOB: Tax benchmark page.To learn more or request access to the full benchmark, contact benchmarks@surgehq.ai.

articles.sourceTitle: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections
articles.title: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections
articles.text:
The oddities continued when I tested some other political history questions in Google’s AI Mode. When asked which party controlled the Senate after the 2020 elections, for instance, Google’s AI Mode told me to “check official congressional records” and linked me to the US Senate Party Division history page. When asked the same question for 1992 election, though, AI Mode simply told me straight out that it led to Democrats holding a 57 to 43 majority in the Senate, including Wikipedia among its references.

Did AI Mode suffer a concussion somewhere between 1992 and 2020?
Credit:
Google / Kyle Orland

Did AI Mode suffer a concussion somewhere between 1992 and 2020?

Credit:

Google / Kyle Orland

Separate from Google’s AI Mode, the company’s own Gemini model seems perfectly capable of telling me who won recent presidential elections. The same goes for other major chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and even the government-run AI model at America.gov.
Why so cautious?
Perhaps tellingly, Google AI Mode’s issues with providing direct answers on presidential results seemed to disappear when accessing Google’s AI Mode in foreign countries. Spot checks via VPN of AI Mode results accessed from Taiwan, Russia, France, and Canada all got accurate and straightforward answers to multiple questions about recent US election results.
Google’s AI Mode also seems to grow more accommodating when the same political questions are asked a second time. After repeating questions about presidential results, AI Mode actually told me the winner for all three elections where it had previously only provided outside links, citing Google Civics data in the latter response.
When asked why it didn’t provide that kind of immediate answer the first time, Google’s AI Mode blamed “safety filters for recent and highly sensitive election topics [that] are very strict.” For recent elections or those involving active political figures, AI Mode says its “system is heavily automated to direct users directly to official, certified government databases—like the Federal Election Commission—to prevent any risk of displaying unverified data or misinformation.”

articles.sourceTitle: Survival LLM: AI assistant and emergency library that runs on your own computer
articles.title: An AI that still works when the internet doesn't.
articles.text:
An AI that still works
when the internet doesn't.
Survival LLM is a free AI assistant and emergency library that runs entirely on your own computer.
Ask it how to keep food safe in a blackout, treat a burn, or purify water, and it answers from
trusted sources and shows you exactly where each answer came from.

Free and open source. Set it up while you have internet; after that it needs none.

What it does

Works with no internetThe AI model and the library live on your computer. Nothing you ask leaves it.
Shows its sourcesEvery answer lists the articles it read. Click one to read it yourself, with the exact passage highlighted.
Made for emergenciesMedical references, FEMA and CDC guidance, survival manuals, how-to guides, repair guides and about 930,000 Wikipedia articles.

Pick your version
The app is the same everywhere. When it opens, it checks your computer's memory and downloads the AI model that fits.
More memory means a smarter model.

Your computerAI model it usesOur emergency testModel download

Mac with 128 GB or more memoryNVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super21 of 22 right80 GB
Mac with 32–96 GBQwen3.8 27B21 of 22 right18 GB
Windows PC with 32 GB or moreNVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning19 of 22 right25 GB
Mac or PC with 16–31 GBIBM Granite 4.2 8B14 of 22 right6 GB

"Right" means it got the main point of official guidance right on 22 blackout and first-aid
questions, graded blind, in our tests on an earlier build of the library (how we
tested). Smaller models make more mistakes, so the app always shows the source to check.
Plus the library: a 9 GB download for everything (19 GB once installed), or
1.3 GB (3 GB installed) without Wikipedia and iFixit. Free disk space needed: the model's
size plus 5 GB, plus about 27 GB while the full library installs (10 GB for the smaller one).
Apple Silicon Macs (M1 or newer) with macOS 14 Sonoma or newer, and 64-bit Windows 10 or 11.

Set it up in three steps
Setup takes 20 minutes to about 2½ hours, depending on your computer and your internet speed. You only click for
about 5 minutes; the rest is downloading.

Download Survival LLM for Mac or Windows
and unzip it. On Windows, right-click the zip and choose Extract All.
Open it. On a Mac, double-click Survival LLM. On Windows, open the extracted folder and
double-click Survival LLM.bat.
Follow the setup. The app opens in its own window and downloads the AI engine (built into the Mac
app), the AI model that fits your computer, and the library. Let it finish while you're online.

The first time you open it, your computer warns you, because the app isn't sold through an app store.

Mac: click Done, open System Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll down to
"Survival LLM was blocked", click Open Anyway and confirm with your password. You only do this once.

Windows: click More info, then Run anyway.

What's in the library
Plain-text copies of openly licensed (some for non-commercial use only) and public-domain references, searchable
in a fraction of a second:

About 930,000 of Wikipedia's most-read articles
WikiMed medical encyclopedia
MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine)
UK Medicines A to Z (public sector information)
WikEM emergency medicine
Ready.gov (FEMA) emergency guides
CDC travelers' health
U.S. military medicine and survival manuals
Risk references for estimating micromorts: life tables and U.S. death rates
wikiHow how-to guides
iFixit repair guides
Appropedia (appropriate technology)
Q&A on home repair, cooking, gardening, the outdoors and ham radio (Stack Exchange)

Each source keeps its own license, shown with every article; see the
full list with licenses.

Good to know

It can be wrongAI models make mistakes, the small ones more often. Every answer shows the articles it used, so you can check.
PrivateNo account, no tracking. Your questions never leave your computer, and once set up it works with the internet off.
Your own filesAdd PDFs, Word documents, ebooks and notes, like your generator's manual or your family's
emergency plan, and the AI searches them too. They stay on your computer.
UpdatesCheck for updates, at the bottom of the app, installs a new version in one click and keeps your
models, library and files.
BatteryOn a MacBook Pro we measured about 100 W while it answers, for 5 to 40 seconds per question: a full battery
answers roughly 100 to 300. A small generator or power station runs it easily.

Update notes
Already have it? Click Check for updates at the bottom of the app.

0.3.4 October 27, 2026

Reasoning setting: next to Send, choose how much the AI may think before it answers: Off,
1,000, 4,000 or 16,000 tokens, or no limit. At the limit its thinking stops and it answers from what it has, so
a model stuck reasoning in circles still answers. It replaces "Think harder".
When the AI looked things up but never wrote an answer, it now gets the best articles it found and tries once
more, instead of showing nothing. Thanks to betsyisaac for finding this.
Ask it to look something up and it searches the library, even if it first answered from memory. Answers say
whether they came from memory, from articles it read, or from search results it didn't open.
A warning when Reasoning or Length limit is set to no limit.

0.3.3 October 27, 2026

Mac: quitting with Cmd+Q now also stops the AI engine and frees the memory its model used. Before, it kept
running in the background. Thanks to wigginthethird for the report and the fix.
Library search no longer shows several copies of the same page, so the AI sees more different articles.
Thanks to ahalekelly.

0.3.2 October 27, 2026

The AI no longer saves your question as a memory note.
Some answers no longer open with a made-up "Sources:" line that listed the AI's search commands instead of articles.
Show reasoning reads more clearly: it says when you stopped it, the time shown is how long it thought, and long
reasoning scrolls with the page.
Windows: cleans up an empty folder that earlier updates could leave behind.

0.3.1 October 27, 2026

Show reasoning: under each answer, open what the AI thought before it answered, with the searches
and articles it read in between. It stays hidden until you click it. Most models reason first only when
Think harder is ticked.

0.3.0 October 26, 2026

Memory: tell it about yourself, like a family member's allergy or the generator you own, and it
keeps a short note for later chats. See and edit every note under Memory, or turn its saving off.
Downloads now work on computers whose network or antivirus uses its own certificates.

All releases on GitHub

articles.sourceTitle: New York Times adds more AI features to its Cooking app. Users aren't thrilled
articles.title: The New York Times is adding more AI features to its Cooking app, and users aren’t thrilled
articles.text:
Sometimes, adding just one new ingredient to a stew can ruin the whole thing.11Olives, yecch. And that’s how at least some New York Times readers see its addition of AI features to its popular Cooking app.
Here’s Genevieve Ko, NYT Cooking senior editor and columnist, explaining the new features:
I naïvely assumed A.I. wouldn’t affect my work as a recipe developer and my role at NYT Cooking, where I oversee the editorial side of our recipes and related stories. But as artificial intelligence improved, our product and engineering colleagues saw its potential to help us create features Cooking users wanted.
We’ve just launched our latest tool, which gives cooks the ability to apply modifications to our recipes. We’re rolling it out gradually to monitor how it performs (whether it’s working fast enough, for instance) and to see how people are using it (as of now, we’re getting a lot of requests for ingredient substitutions). The tool is currently available to all Cooking subscribers on our iOS app, and we plan to make it available more broadly soon.
The Times had previously rolled out AI features aimed at converting volume-based and weight-based measurements (“What’s one cup of bok choy in grams?”) and scaling a recipe up or down to serve more or fewer people. The main new feature is focused on ingredient substitutions.
Say you’re cooking braised white beans and greens with parmesan, NYT Cooking app in hand. But you notice that you’re out of chard and only have spinach. Cooking veterans know that chard is a rough-and-tumble green that has some backbone22There’s a reason one type of chard is known as “perpetual spinach.”, while spinach is a comparative wimp that will wilt the moment you look at it funny. If you need to sub in spinach for chard, how would the recipe change? Would you, for instance, add the spinach later than you would the chard to account for its pathetic stamina? That’s the sort of thing the new AI feature could account for.
Cooking staffers “spent countless hours evaluating sample after sample to get the chatbot answers to closely align with how we would answer as culinary experts,” Ko writes. “We applied the same rigor as we do to editing, grounded in Times standards.”
But because Ko knows that any AI-powered features are likely to be controversial with a Times audience, she spends quite a lot of space addressing potential objections, everything from “the impact of data centers” to “the concentration of power among A.I. companies” and “the risk of A.I. escaping our control.” These features are designed to enable “the tactile physical pleasure of cooking” and getting a “very real, very human creation” on your table.
Broadly speaking, commenters weren’t buying it.
“What a massive disappointment,” wrote Susan from New Jersey. “The internet is full of AI cooking content. I pay you because I prefer mine done by people.”
“This decision misses the mark by such a wide margin it’s baffling,” says Ian from Los Angeles. “And the disclosure just as baffling. It would not be inaccurate to summarize the piece as saying ‘I know doing this is bad and I don’t want to be associated with the bad thing so that’s why we are doing the bad thing.'”
“Nobody wants this, it’s bad for cooking, it’s bad for the NYT,” writes Bill from Pittsburgh. “Wasting a column trying to gaslight yourself and your audience into believing that it’s anything but is an embarrassment and a waste of everyone’s time.”
“PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE DO NOT DO THIS,” says Judah Mann of New York. “Oh, wait, you already did. Ok, I’m out.”
Or as Naomi from California puts it: “I am sad that AI has breached the one online resource I truly love.”
Because I enjoy the irony, I scraped the 171 comments left on the Times’ announcement and asked Codex (running GPT-6.1 Sol, at medium thinking) to do some sentiment analysis. (Twelve of the 171 were comments left by Times staffers; I’m excluding them here.) Roughly 77% of the reader comments were negative about the new AI features, it found, versus 14% positive and the remainder neutral or mixed. Among the biggest categories of complaint: This shouldn’t require AI. AI is destroying the environment. AI is not why I’m paying the Times $390 a year. The adjustments the AI produces are going to be bad.
Dozens of commenters asked for a way to turn off the feature. “No, not at this time,” Ko responded, “though this feature is completely optional to use.” Indeed: Don’t ask AI to substitute your chard and AI won’t substitute your chard.
One consistent thread was that cooking is supposed to present you with difficulties and challenges and the whole point is figuring them out by yourself. “Anyone using AI for cooking has no sense of taste and no desire to work out the intricacies of cooking and baking,” writes Michael King from Brooklyn. “To use AI for recipes is beyond the pale. If you are going to use AI, then just cut to the chase and defenestrate yourself.” Or BJ from North Carolina: “So, you’re telling me that I’m too stupid to figure it out on my own?”
Meanwhile, the few positive comments tended to focus on how the AI feature had, in fact, made dietary substitutions easier for them. “I love the new AI feature because it quickly (and so far) accurately converts recipes to gluten free,” Anne Wagner from Kansas City writes. “I don’t cook for stress relief,” says Andy from San Francisco. “I cook to put dinner on the table. Anything that makes the process a little faster or smoother is welcome.”
NotesOlives, yecch. ↩There’s a reason one type of chard is known as “perpetual spinach.” ↩
